Ruthie Cecelia Foster (born February 10, 1964) is an American singer-songwriter of blues and folk music. She mixes a wide palette of American song forms, from gospel and blues to jazz, folk and soul. She has often been compared to Bonnie Raitt and Aretha Franklin. Foster has been nominated for multiple Grammy Awards for Best Blues Album and Best Contemporary Blues Album, and won her first Grammy on February 2, 2025.

Foster is from Gause, Texas, and comes from a family of gospel singers. At the age of fourteen, Foster was a soloist in her hometown choir and was certain that her future would revolve around music. After high school, she moved to Waco, Texas, and she began fronting a blues band, learning how to command a stage in the bars of Texas. Hoping to travel and gain a wider world perspective, Foster joined the United States Navy, and soon began singing in the naval band Pride which played pop and funk hits at recruitment drives.

Following her tour of duty, Foster headed to New York City where she became a regular performer at various local folk venues. Atlantic Records heard of Foster's talent and offered her a recording deal with the intent of cultivating her as a budding pop star, but Foster was not interested in a pop career. When her mother fell ill in 1993, Foster left New York and returned to Texas while she cared for her mother who died in 1996.

In 1997, Foster self-released the album Full Circle, the success of which paved the way to a long relationship with the record label Blue Corn Music. Foster's awards list includes three Grammy nominations (Let It Burn for Best Blues Album, The Truth According to Ruthie Foster for Best Contemporary Blues Album, and Promise of a Brand New Day for Best Blues Album), her numerous wins at the Blues Music Awards, including three awards for Best Female Vocalist and one for DVD of the Year for Live At Antone's, and Foster's crown for Best Female Vocalist at the 2013 Austin Music Awards. Foster earned the 2025 Grammy Award for Best Contemporary Blues Album for her album Mileage, her 13th album. She continues to tour and her shows have spanned across the U.S., Italy, Germany, Spain, and Cuba.

#2666. Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 11 of NCAA Football Season

Welcome back to another installment of Future Broncos. Last week, I focused on a trio of defenders for Broncos Country to keep their eye on as the rest of the collegiate football season transpires. This week, I'll switch gears and offer three players on offense since that side of the ball has been Denver's biggest issue in 2026.

So far this season, I've offered my thoughts on a handful of offensive line prospects. Mizzou's Cayden Green, Indiana's Carter Smith, Minnesota's Greg Johnson, and USC's Elijah Paige. Based on the comments section, identifying more big guys in the offensive trenches is something you are all interested in.

Georgia fifth-year senior Earnest Green III has been on my radar for a while. Back in 2023, he was a fourteen-game starter for the Bulldogs at left tackle protecting future top pick Carson Beck. He continued to man down that position for nine games in 2024, but a lingering shoulder issue cost him a few games and slowed the promise he showed as a freshman.

Last season, Greene (6'4″, 320 pounds) flipped to right tackle while Monroe Freeling was manning the blindside. However, he started just nine games due to lingering back issues. Though he didn't give up a sack in the over 800 offensive snaps he played in 2005.

Now healthy, Greene is back home where it all started on the left side of Georgia's stalwart offensive line. The redshirt senior is poised to finish his collegiate career with over 40 starts and over 3,000 snaps between both tackle positions and having three different line coaches. That experience will pay off and mean a lot to NFL scouts and general managers who value experience and top-notch SEC pedigrees.

I'm a big fan of the depth he gets in his pass sets. I also like his ability to anchor and hold his own against strong power rushers. Moreover, I am impressed with his ability to get up field and take on blockers at the second level. It'll be interesting to see how he measures [arm length] during the pre-draft circuit. There are some who believe his best football is inside at guard, but I think he can stick at tackle.

Last week's performance versus Ole Miss earned him the Outland Trophy Player of the Week honors. To date, Greene has only given up four quarterback pressures on the season. The Broncos could use a tough and battle-tested player in their trenches next April, and I believe Greene (if medicals check out) has a shot at being a Day 2 selection. You can catch him in action this afternoon on ABC when the top-ranked Bulldogs host Mizzou.

For most of my Future Broncos installments, I've tried to focus on seniors whether it be fourth or fifth-year players. One particular reason is that NIL money has changed the NFL Draft landscape. Early declarations are basically half of what they used to be. In turn, that makes it a lot harder to find quality players to address needs.

However, a potential early round pick that may wind up declaring early if he keeps playing well is Notre Dame offensive lineman Anthonie Knapp. He manned down the left tackle position for the Fighting Irish for the first 27 games of his collegiate career. For his third season, the junior has kicked inside to guard.

That's where many analysts have stated his best NFL potential might be. However, there are a handful of others who think a further kick inside to the pivot may be where he blossoms. Regardless, his versatility will be a big enhancer for his draft stock if he chooses to declare.

We all know Head Coach Sean Payton values experience and versatility when it comes to offensive lineman. This Golden Domer certainly fits the bill. By the end of this season, Knapp (6'5", 305 pounds) will have logged well over 2,000 snaps and have three full seasons of starting experience.

While he could stand to put on some weight and muscle to handle the rigors of the pro game, his anchor is incredibly strong at this stage. In my opinion, he plays with NFL ready technique at the line of scrimmage. He has been an enforcer in the run game and a key reason for Notre Dame's success on the ground this season. As a pass protector, Knapp has been credited with giving up just one sack in nearly three dozen starts.

Whether or not Knapp chooses to declare remains to be seen but given Denver's long-term needs at multiple positions on the offensive line, he would be a quality prospect for them to consider. I believe he has a legitimate shot to be a Top 50 player easily if he decides to take his talents to the NFL. You can watch him in action when the third-ranked Fighting Irish host Boston College this afternoon.

Thus far in our Future Broncos installments, we have highlighted just two tight ends in the 2027 NFL Draft. Underclassmen Oregon's Jamari Johnson and Virginia Tech's Luke Reynolds. I have a strong feeling both of them will declare and will merit early consideration by NFL teams looking to upgrade the position.

This collegiate season, another underclassman from Iowa is making quite the statement this season—DJ Vonnahme. Over the years, the Hawkeyes have been a tight end producing factory under Kirk Ferentz. Players like George Kittle, Noah Fant, T.J. Hockensen, and Sam LaPorta all come to mind.

Vonnahme (6'4", 241 pounds) appears to be next to follow in their footsteps. Appearing in twelve games as a redshirt freshman in 2025, Vonnahme logged five starts and was the Hawkeyes' leading receiver with 29 catches, 434 yards, and 3 touchdowns. He popped onto the map of scouts last season with a dominant seven catch, 146-yard performance against Vanderbilt in last year's ReliaQuest Bowl.

In eight games in 2026, Vonnahme sports 32 receptions for 314 yards and 3 touchdowns as well as one rushing touchdown. His yards per route ran (2.59) is amongst the highest in the nation. He has one of the best contested catch rates in the nation and can work multiple levels of the field.

While there is no doubting his upside and talent as a receiving threat at the next level, Vonnahme's work as a blocker leaves a lot to be desired. It's important to note he is only 20 years old and is a former quarterback that is still learning the nuances of the position. Getting better at blocking is something he can certainly get better at with more time.

Vonnahme is just a redshirt sophomore. With that in mind, a return back to Iowa seems quite likely. Though with this year's class not having a clear-cut number one just yet, perhaps he goes pro if he gets good enough feedback in the pre-draft process. You can catch him in tonight when the sixteenth ranked Hawkeyes host Purdue tomorrow evening on NBC.

#2665. MLB free agency: Six international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball's free agency period opened earlier this week and teams are now clear to pursue any roster upgrades they deem necessary. That includes players coming over from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league, South Korea's Korea Baseball Organization, and Taiwan's Chinese Professional Baseball League. Those are high-level leagues that have sent many impact players MLB's way over the years.

Look no farther than the Dodgers to see how important international talent can be to a club. The Dodgers employed four different former NPB and KBO players this past season, including two-way star Shohei Ohtani, ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and starter Roki Sasaki. Ohtani was signed as an MLB free agent, but the others went to the Dodgers through the posting system.

Per the posting agreement with MLB, posted NPB and CPBL players get a 45-day window to negotiate and sign with an MLB team. KBO players get a 30-day window. Players who do not sign during that posting window return to their previous team in NPB, CPBL, or KBO. The MLB team that signs a posted player pays a fee to the player's former NPB, CPBL, or KBO team.

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Munetaka Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract last offseason. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Unlike last lockout, MLB will not be pausing the signing window during the expected lockout, according to The Athletic. In other words, if owners lock players out on Dec. 1 as expected, that date will essentially serve as the same deadline for already posted NPB players unless the lockout ends before their 45-day window expires.

There are no superstar-caliber players like Ohtani or Yamamoto available in this winter's international free agent crop. There are, however, several interesting players who can improve an MLB roster in 2027. Here are the six best NPB, CPBL, and KBO players to know this offseason.

Japan's Triple Crown winner hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. He has a similar skill set to Murakami but is not exactly Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games in 2026 around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll. The Hanshin Tigers officially posted Sato on Nov. 1.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Itoh on Nov. 1.

Roh has an unusual agreement with the Hanwha Eagles. He signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and roughly $23 million), and as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him for MLB teams this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the Eagles to finish his career when his big-league stint is over. This past season, Roh, 26 in November, authored a .283/.360/.505 batting line with 29 home runs. He has real right-handed power and a good approach at the plate. There are concerns about his propensity to swing and miss as well as his arm at the hot corner. The Eagles formally posted Roh on Nov. 1.

The Seibu Lions posted Takahashi last offseason, but he was unable to find a contract to his liking, so he returned to Japan for another season and threw 148 innings with a 2.64 ERA. Takahashi, 30 in February, is an international free agent now, meaning he does not have to be posted and can instead negotiate at his own pace. More of a ground ball pitcher than a bat-misser, Takahashi sits in the 91-95 mph range with his fastball and has two good secondary pitches in his slider and splitter. He also throws a cutter and curveball. Takahashi is considered a potential innings guy for the back of an MLB rotation.

Tseng pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026 and he has been one of the CPBL's top relievers the last few years. In 2026, he saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s and has run as high as 100 mph in the past, though it has been a few years. His go-to secondary pitch is a breaking ball that needs improvement for Tseng to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2662. ‘Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles

'Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker shared the floor for 128 games in Portland. The Trail Blazers won 43 of them.

They sat beside one another in the Sixers' interview room Thursday night after a victory and discussed what the other 85 taught them.

"Whether you've got a big role or a small role, it's hard to win in the NBA," Simons said. "We've seen it firsthand."

Their roles were considerably different then.

Simons was an established starter entrusted with creating and scoring. Walker, a 2022 second-round pick, was trying to establish himself in a rotation. During their three overlapping seasons, Portland went 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46. The Blazers missed the playoffs each year.

Both are now reserves on a Sixers team constructed to contend. In nine games they've both appeared in this season, Philadelphia is 7-2.

They provided 26 points, 11 rebounds and six three-pointers in the Sixers' 123-112 win over the Raptors at Xfinity Mobile Arena. Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range. Walker recorded nine points and eight rebounds, including four on the offensive glass.

The Sixers outscored Toronto by 24 points during Simons' 23 minutes. Neither former Blazer committed a turnover.

Their production helped Philadelphia overcome a 17-point first-quarter deficit and improve to 10-3 without LeBron James.

"You learn once you come off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there," Simons said. "Obviously, we started off kind of slow. You just want to go in, bring some energy, get some stops, get out and run. I think everybody who got off the bench brought energy."

Simons supplied an immediate lift with a deep three-pointer at the first-quarter buzzer. His shot ended an 8-0 Sixers run and trimmed Toronto's lead to nine.

He remained involved during an 11-0 burst late in the third quarter, knocking down a three and setting up Walker for a basket. Walker then made a three early in the fourth before Simons scored on the Sixers' next possession.

When Toronto pulled within six with less than five minutes remaining, Simons answered with his fifth three-pointer.

Making those shots is the most obvious way Simons can help a roster already featuring James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown. He said the Sixers have not made him feel as though every opportunity must go in.

"They encourage us to keep shooting the ball," Simons said. "Knowing that a team has that much confidence in us to keep shooting makes the game that much easier. Whether you miss or make, as long as we get the right shots in the right moments, I think everybody can live with the misses and makes."

Simons spent seven seasons in Portland before playing last year with Boston and Chicago. His move to Philadelphia reunited him with Walker and Rayan Rupert, another former Blazer who joined the Sixers on a two-way contract during the offseason.

Knowing familiar faces awaited him helped Simons enter another new locker room.

"It made the transition seamless," he said. "Just being able to have some comfortability with guys that I played with for multiple years. It's been fun, kind of feeling like a little bit of old times. Me, Bari and Rups have been through a lot."

Walker's path to Philadelphia began a year earlier and required an additional step.

After playing 188 games over three seasons with Portland, Walker signed a two-way contract with the Sixers in July 2025. He earned a standard contract in February and has since pushed his way into the backup-center conversation despite standing 6-foot-7.

Walker believes some of the work he did on losing teams was easily missed.

"When I first got to the league, I was part of a rebuilding process," he said. "I just felt like some of the little things I did didn't always get noticed when you're losing. I told myself, if I ever got to be part of a winning organization, then I'd go out and expand my abilities."

Rebounding has made Walker difficult for Nick Nurse to overlook.

Walker credited his timing and strong hands to lessons passed down by his father, former NBA center Samaki Walker. Those instincts have become especially useful while the Sixers piece together their frontcourt behind Embiid.

"Rebounding is a skill I kind of honed in on," Walker said. "My dad was a good rebounder. He was known for his rebounding and his timing. I think it's just a gift that he transferred to me."

Walker has made it clear that he expected to earn a role this season.

"I don't know if I was delusional, but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part," he said. "I read something where they said it's a surprise, but if you were around me this summer, it wouldn't be a surprise. This is expected, and I just want to continue to get better."

The freedom Simons once had in Portland is no longer necessary. Walker does not need a high volume of touches, either. Both understand that playing beside the Sixers' stars requires shooting when open, moving the ball and handling the less glamorous work.

"You've got to find ways to impact the game multiple ways, even if you're not scoring," Simons said. "Whether it's cutting, making the right read and pass to Joel, being the right swing pass to VJ, boxing out on defense or just being in the right position."

Their opportunities will fluctuate. Simons may take nine shots one night and only a few the next. Walker's minutes will depend on matchups and the health of Philadelphia's frontcourt.

Winning has changed what they are being asked to do. Their three years together in Portland taught them why the adjustment is worthwhile.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something you can't take for granted."

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2660. Malik Beasley Sells Signed NBA Jerseys on TikTok Weeks Before Guilty Plea in Gambling Case

Malik Beasley opened up his collection of NBA jerseys to TikTok viewers on Wednesday night, offering memorabilia from his playing career for sale. The former Detroit Pistons guard fielded questions while holding up uniforms, including pieces from his early years with the Denver Nuggets.

The November 11 livestream came as the 29-year-old prepares to plead guilty in a federal sports betting case. His attorney, Steve Haney, confirmed the agreement on October 27, with a court appearance still ahead.

Basketball accounts including NBACentral and MrBuckBuckNBA circulated clips the following day. The footage drew attention to keepsakes from a career that spanned nine NBA seasons and six teams.

Beasley has not explained in the circulated footage whether the sale is connected to legal bills or other expenses. The recordings offer no reliable picture of his current finances or how much money he received.

Wearing a Denver uniform himself, Beasley told viewers he would personalize the items they bought. "Once you get it I will sign them myself and put your name on it," he said, according to Complex. The Nuggets selected him with the 19th overall pick in the 2016 NBA Draft.

He was less willing to part with a Minnesota Timberwolves jersey. When a viewer asked about one, Beasley acknowledged that he had it but said he wanted to keep it.

He joined Minnesota in a February 2020 trade and spent parts of three seasons there, averaging 19.6 points across 37 games in 2020-21. Minnesota traded him to the Utah Jazz in July 2022, followed by stops with the Los Angeles Lakers and Milwaukee Bucks before Detroit.

Beasley's change-of-plea hearing is scheduled for December 9 in Brooklyn federal court, Bloomberg reported. He initially pleaded not guilty on July 1, according to the Los Angeles Times.

An indictment unsealed June 29 named five other defendants, including former NBA forward Ed Davis and player agent Paolo Zamorano. The charges included wire fraud conspiracy, bribery in sporting contests, honest services wire fraud conspiracy and money laundering conspiracy.

According to the Justice Department, Beasley agreed to manipulate selected statistics while playing for Milwaukee during the 2023-24 season. Prosecutors allege that Davis passed advance information about his intended performance to others, enabling them to place bets tied to those statistics.

The indictment identified four games involving Cleveland, Charlotte, the Clippers and Brooklyn. For the February 27, 2024, Charlotte game, prosecutors described a plan to score fewer points while collecting more rebounds than the relevant betting lines anticipated. They said Beasley's compensation typically took the form of reductions or payments toward gambling debts he owed Davis.

Beasley's most recent NBA season had made him a significant contributor to Detroit's offense. He played all 82 regular-season games in 2024-25 and averaged 16.3 points, helping the Pistons return to the playoffs for the first time since 2019.

His 319 three-pointers set a franchise record, as the Pistons noted in their season review. He finished second in Sixth Man of the Year voting behind Boston's Payton Pritchard.

Detroit was discussing a three-year, $42 million contract with Beasley when the federal investigation became public in June 2025. Those negotiations were put on hold, Local 4 reported. The proposed agreement was never completed.

#2659. Rams vs. Arizona Cardinals: How to watch, start time, odds and prediction

Myles Garrett is coming off a dominating three-sack performance in his return to the Rams' lineup.

"Not a 100 [%]," he told reporters Friday when asked to put a percentage-gauge on how he felt in last Sunday's victory over the Washington Commanders. "I can't go that far. We're not a 100 but we're trying to make our way there."

Garrett, who sat out seven games while recovering from left knee surgery, is listed as questionable for Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals. But he is expected to play as the Rams attempt to extend their winning streak to four games.

The two-time NFL defensive player of the year's influence on the team extends beyond the field.

In the locker room, the 10th-year pro is the top-rated player in a player-organized, no-contact shadow-boxing league designed to instill competition and camaraderie.

Garrett, who spent his first nine seasons with the Cleveland Browns, said he didn't bring the competition with him, "but I will say I was the top dog where I left and top dog now, so not much has changed."

Garrett said he does not back down from a challenge by teammates.

Coach Sean McVay welcomes the team-building component of the competition.

"It's always about when can you find those times to lock in but when can you do those things that organically occur to create a camaraderie and a connection that is something that only the players can really be able to do," McVay said. "When you're hearing laughs, I think that's the sign of a good culture."

Garrett played 37 of 62 defensive snaps against the Commanders and said he was "tired as hell" afterward.

After the Rams play the Cardinals, they will have what will essentially be a mini-bye before playing the Green Bay Packers on the night before Thanksgiving.

Garrett said the bye was coming at "a perfect time" for all players.

"Being able to get some extra practice myself, being on the field and being able to train and work on some things, get in my rhythm even without some games, I think will help us all in the long run," he said.

Rams: OL Steve Avila (hamstring, out); TE Terrance Ferguson (hamstring, out); Myles Garrett (knee, questionable), CB Trent McDuffie (back, questionable); S Kam Curl (toe, questionable); TE Davis Allen (oblique, questionable); LS Joe Cardona (ankle, questionable).

It will be available nationally via a subscription to NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube TV. In Southern California, fans can listen to the game on 710 AM, 93.1 FM and 1330 AM (Español).

Gary Klein's prediction: The Rams are missing star receivers Puka Nacua and Davante Adams, but Garrett and defensive lineman Aaron Donald will terrorize quarterback Carson Beck in his first NFL game. Rams 27, Cardinals 17

#2655. Big Blue View mailbag: Kickoff rule, Rasul Douglas interception, more

Lou Catalano asks: Could you please explain the rule concerning kickoffs going out of bounds? In the Giants/Washington game, the ball bounced in bounds, the returner stepped out of bounds, then caught the ball while his knee was touching the ground in bounds. What ever happpened to the old John Madden maxim that one knee equals two feet?

Ed says: Lou, you weren't the only confused by this. The rulebook says:

"A ball that is in player possession is out of bounds when the runner is out of bounds."

On kickoffs, this is a bit of a loophole. Credit Luke McCaffrey of the Commanders for knowing the rule and making a great play. If you plant your feet out of bounds, then touch a ball that is inbounds, it makes the ball considered to be out of bounds. That creates a kickoff out of bounds and puts the ball at the 40-yard line.

I have seen this happen a couple of times. I have also seen players mess this up by either catching the ball and stepping out of bounds, or by picking the ball up inbounds right near the sideline and trying to return it.

David Silver asks: I'm trying to make sense out of the last throw JJ McCarthy made to Nabers that was intercepted. It looks like McCarthy hung the ball up based on the trajectory. It also gave Nabers plenty of time to get it sighted. Douglas comes from behind to high point Nabers, but it also looked like he hit Nabers early. But that is a 50/50 ball Nabers wants. My question is, bad throw, bad catch attempt, great defensive play, or pass interference?

Ed says: David, sometimes you just have to give the other guy credit. I have watched this play a bunch of times, and I listened to Nabers and John Harbaugh talk about it on Friday.

Washington sent a zero blitz, rushing more players than the Giants could block and forcing J.J. McCarthy to make a split-second decision. His decision was to give the Giants' best receiver a chance to make a play. Right decision? Wrong decision? Harbaugh just said it was the decision that McCarthy made. Douglas didn't interfere with Nabers. Nabers said he was focused on tracking the ball and knew there was a defender in the area, but didn't know where. Douglas did not interfere with Nabers. He just ended up making a play.

The Giants have won a couple of games like that this season. The other guys get paid, too.

Raymond Dansereau asks: How much better are the Giants really than last year? Last year they had a tough schedule and close losses; this year, they're playing a weak schedule and really not always looking great. Defense seems better, but is this a 10-7 playoffs team that gets beaten badly in the first round? Or, does this look like sustainable improvement? Or too soon to say?

Ed says: Raymond, I can't go position-by-position or player-by-player in a mailbag response. I think the real answer is that the Giants are better simply because they have John Harbaugh and they are coached better. It doesn't hurt that this team has Arvell Reese, either.

The Giants are winning close games, which they couldn't do last year. A lot of that is coaching, whether it is in-game decisions or just preparing players well enough that they believe they are supposed to make plays and win close games.

If it is a 9-7-1 playoff team that gets bounced in the first round, what's wrong with that? The Giants won seven games combined the past two seasons — a playoff berth would be a fantastic accomplishment. Sustainable improvement? The NFL is such a week-to-week and year-to-year league that is impossible to say. As long as Harbaugh is the coach, though, the Giants have a chance to be relevant. That is a massive improvement.

Matt Smith asks: We've had four failures in a row at the head coach position. They are bookended by two Hall of Fame coaches. My question is, seeing how far the gap is between Daboll and Harbaugh, do you find it surprising how long we waited to move on from him? It seems more and more apparent to me that we had talent that we could've done with if we had a professional head coach with standards. The red flags were always there.

Ed says: Matt, I'm not at all surprised that the Giants waited as long as they did to move on from Brian Daboll. look at the Giants' track record:

Ben McAdoo lasted less than two full seasons.

Joe Judge was fired (well, he kinda fired himself) after two seasons.

You cannot get ahead when you have to keep blowing things up and starting over every two years. That means an entire new coaching staff, gutting most of the roster, and starting over. You can never institute a real philosophy or build anything that way.

John Mara knew it, and he said several times that he knew he needed to be more patient than he had been.

Daboll had a shockingly good first season and won Coach of the Year. The Giants could have justified firing him and GM Joe Schoen after a 3-14 2024 season, but chose not to.

Mike Vrabel got hired by New England that offseason. Zero chance he was picking the Giants over the Patriots, the team he played for an an organization he loves. Ben Johnson got hired by the Bears. No chance he was picking the Giants over the Bears, who already had Caleb Williams in place. Liam Coen got hired by the Jaguars, but nobody knew that would work out as well as it had.

It was really the 2025 season when it became clear that the coaching staff wasn't maximizing the talent of the players.

Adam Singer asks: During the game against the Eagles, it looked like some of the players had a diagonal line through the word "GIANTS" on their helmets while others did not. What was going on there?

Ed says: Adam, the word 'GIANTS' was underlined. I think what you saw was the chinstrip, which buckles on the side of the helmet, protruding over the lettering on some of the helmets.

Ronald Lukoff asks: I usually do not disagree with a lot of your comments but I do take exception to your thoughts about the Giants making a blockbuster trade today (this is written Tuesday morning). I have been a Giant fan since 1956. I have seen a lot of success and a lot of failure. This team is made up of a lot of draft picks and I really do not want to give up future draft choices for a player that can give us a division title. This team has only played one team with a record above .500. Do you really think that one player is worth losing draft capital? If I thought one player could get us to the Super Bowl, I might feel differently. Do you think JJ is the answer at QB. He was great first 5 quarters, not so much last game. but a quarterback needy ream just traded him away, so I am hesitant to put all my faith in him and believe me, I hope I'm wrong. I feel like we are at least a year away from potentially going to the Super Bowl and while I would love to win the division, I just don't think giving up draft choices is the best way to build a championship team. You're feelings?

Ed says: Ronald, it's moot at this point since the trade deadline has come and gone. I want to clarify this, anyway.

I wrote earlier in the week that the Giants should try to capitalize on the opportunity they have in the NFC East. You don't know if or when that opportunity will come again.

They did try to do that. They were very aggressive. They were also careful. I said earlier in the week there was a price they should not go to — meaning they should not go above the second-round pick they had offered the Colts for Jonathan Taylor. They — rightly — refused to do that.

I said all along the end game is not winning the division this year and then going back to being a third- or fourth-place team for fove years after that. The end game is to be a championship contender on a consistent basis. You have to protect your future to do that.

#2654. MLB rumors: Why the Dodgers could be Tarik Skubal or bust; Red Sox looking for pitching depth

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest thing hanging over baseball this offseason is obviously the expiration of the CBA and what everyone assumes will be a lockout. Until then, we'll find out the major award winners this coming week, starting with Rookies of the Year on Monday. And, of course, there's the player movement yet to come.

For the latter, let's round up Sunday's rumors right here.

As we saw plenty in 2026, the Dodgers have a very talented rotation with a few injury-prone parts (Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher, etc.). As such, this bit of speculative reporting from The Athletic makes a ton of sense:

The Dodgers will need someone who can cover innings in 2027. It's just a matter of how much they can lean on Justin Wrobleski, trust how Emmet Sheehan finished the season (I'd say probably a good amount), how healthy Gavin Stone is (unknown), how ready Jackson Ferris is (he seems close) and if they have enough depth options behind them.

All that to say, the Dodgers will be in on Skubal. If he goes elsewhere, I don't think it's as simple as the Dodgers going after the next highest-ranked starter on the market, such as a Freddy Peralta or a Michael King. I could see them taking a flier on some depth options to soak up innings in anticipation of a quick ramp-up post-lockout, sort of like they did when they signed Tyler Anderson in the run-up to the 2022 season.

Yes, the Dodgers are in on the Tarik Skubal bidding. We all know that. But if they lose out on retaining the two-time Cy Young winner, they may not just continue moving down the list for available starters. Then again, it's hard to ever know exactly what Andrew Friedman is going to spend money on.

As things stand, the Dodgers' rotation has Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow, Roki Sasaki and Sheehan, at least until Ohtani is ready to rejoin the fray.

Coming off two straight Wild Card Series losses and sub-90-win seasons, the Red Sox would surely like to take things up a notch for the 2027 season. One way might be to build out the depth of the pitching staff. They'll be "in the market for a back-end starter" and a right-handed reliever "with swing-and-miss capability," according to MassLive.

For the rotation: Sonny Gray hits free agency, but Garrett Crochet will return from a nearly full-season injury. Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez fill the 2-3 spots, with Jake Bennett solid as the No. 4. That leaves Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford and Tanner Houck as options for the fifth spot in addition to depth. It doesn't seem dire, but we've seen plenty of times what kind of havoc injuries can wreak.

In the bullpen, lefty Aroldis Chapman returns at closer with Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller as setup men. Houck missing out on a rotation spot could mean he helps late as well.

#2652. MLB rumors: Why the Cubs may already be out on Tarik Skubal, plus latest on Phillies, Cardinals, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are already flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Monday's supply just below.

The expectation remains that we'll see some level of activity on the trade and free agency fronts before the lockout begins in early December. As noted above, that was indeed the case leading up to the last lockout, and this time around, the prospect of drastic changes in the next CBA may have big-spending teams looking to fortify their rosters before those changes are implemented. Speaking of which, MLB Network reports that we could see some notable transactions go down at the upcoming General Managers Meetings, which take place from Nov. 10-12 in Las Vegas.

During a standard offseason, not much beyond behind-the-scenes groundwork goes down during the GM Meetings, and the real moves start happening at the December Winter Meetings. However, unless the lockout is resolved quickly – highly unlikely – then there probably won't be a Winter Meetings this offseason. That means the GM Meetings could be more active than usual.

Free agent ace and, until later this week, reigning back-to-back  American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal is the prize of the offseason. The 29-year-old lefty is a fit for any of MLB's 30 teams, but heretofore the most serious bidders have been expected to be the Los Angeles Dodgers (who acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers leading up to last season's trade deadline), the New York Mets, and the Chicago Cubs. Now, though, perhaps you can reduce that number of serious bidders to two. While Chicago very much needs rotation help for 2027 and beyond, the Athletic reports that the Cubs "are expected to stay on the sidelines" when the Skubal bidding gets serious. That, no doubt, will come as a disappointment to Cubs fans who are still waiting for the Ricketts to invest in the payroll at levels befitting a big-market contender.

The Cardinals traded away veteran lefty reliever JoJo Romero, along with starter and fellow free agent Dustin May, to the Milwaukee Brewers leading up to the trade deadline. Now, St. Louis may be interested in bringing Romero back on a free agent contract, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports.

Romero, 30, is coming off a 2026 season in which he pitched to a 3.36 ERA with a 3.00 K/BB ratio in 55 appearances. In the postseason with Milwaukee, Romero had a 1.13 ERA with 11 strikeouts and one walk in eight innings. He previously spent parts of five seasons with the Cardinals.

Do the Philadelphia Phillies need a new shortstop? That's one of the principal questions of their offseason. Although incumbent Trea Turner is signed through 2033, his defense at the crucial position of shortstop has degraded into "unplayable" territory, and that has the Phils considering fallback options should Turner need to be moved off the position. One option is free agent 31-year-old Ha-Seong Kim, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports. Kim, 32, spent last season on a one-year deal with the division-rival Atlanta Braves. He's been a primary shortstop for five of his six MLB seasons, and while he's certainly not among the very best at the position, he does profile as a major defensive upgrade over Turner. As for the bat, Kim for his career has an OPS+ of 93, and he's capable of stealing a base on occasion. He was, however, an offensive sinkhole for 51 games in 2026. Turner, meantime, may be looking at a switch to the outfield starting next season as the Phillies attempt to keep their contending window open.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2650. Predicting 2027 MLB Rookie of the Year candidates: Josue De Paula, Kade Anderson, Jesús Made and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle and Reds slugger Sal Stewart were named the 2026 Rookies of the Year on Monday night. McGonigle was the wire-to-wire leader for the award despite a stacked American League rookie class. In the National League, Stewart edged out Mets outfielder Carson Benge and Cardinals second baseman JJ Wetherholt, both of whom had excellent rookie campaigns.

No award gets you excited about the future the way Rookie of the Year does. It's a young player being recognized for his greatness, and great young players are what sports hopes are built on. With that in mind, here's a look ahead at the 2027 rookie class and, more importantly, who could be in the running for the 2027 Rookie of the Year awards.

Anderson made his debut in late August and gave the Mariners seven solid starts, though he remains rookie-eligible because he did not exceed the rookie limits of 50 innings or 45 days of service time. Anderson, the No. 3 pick in the 2025 Draft, is arguably the best pitching prospect in the game and is likely to have a rotation spot on Opening Day, which figures to boost his Rookie of the Year case. Add in a pitcher-friendly home ballpark, and Anderson is the super early favorite for the award. He had 167 strikeouts against only 22 walks in 129 innings between MLB and the minors in 2026.

One of the best prospects in the minors, Arias nearly made his MLB debut in September, but the Red Sox opted against it. He authored a .323/.400/.557 line with 25 home runs between Double-A and Triple-A in 2026, including a .331/.388/.506 line in 42 games at Triple-A as a 20-year-old. Trevor Story is entering the final year of his contract and has been healthy and productive at the same time once in the last four years. Arias likely gives Boston a better chance to win right now and I would not be surprised to see them turn the shortstop reins over to the youngster early next season. Early as in April.

Like Anderson, Jenkins made his MLB debut in late August, yet his rookie eligibility remains intact going into 2027. He had a rough go of it in the majors, slashing .226/.293/.393 in 26 games with the Twins, though his contact rates and plate discipline were impressive. Jenkins will turn only 22 in February and he is not the first top prospect to have a rough 26 games to begin his big-league career, nor will he be the last. There might be more growing pains to come next season, but Minnesota figures to give Jenkins a long runway to work through them. His 2027 could look like Benge's 2026, meaning sluggish early and sensational late.

It was only 11 games (plus four pinch-hitting appearances in the postseason), but gosh, De Paula was so impressive during his big-league debut. He's a precocious hitter with tremendous strike zone knowledge (13 walks and five strikeouts), and also some serious hard-hit ability. The biggest obstacle standing between De Paula and next year's Rookie of the Year award is playing time. Shohei Ohtani is locked in at DH and Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker aren't going anywhere. The Dodgers will have to either trade or bench Teoscar Hernández to get De Paula into the lineup. It would be worth it. The Yordan Alvarez comps De Paula got in the minors don't seem so insane now.

The Brewers are the World Series champions and they also have arguably the best farm system in the game with the consensus No. 1 prospect in Made. Still only 19, Made performed admirably in a full season at Double-A this year, and he's currently playing very well against grown men in the Dominican Winter League. He figures to open next season in Triple-A, with a May or June promotion to Milwaukee in the cards. That could put Made at a disadvantage in the Rookie of the Year race. Either way, it's only a matter of time until the defending champions add the game's best prospect to their lineup, presumably at third base.

At 20 years and 121 days, Salas became the youngest catcher to ever appear in a postseason game in Game 2 of this year's Wild Card Series. He started three of San Diego's six postseason games after making his MLB debut in September, and it seems likely Salas will take over as their starting backstop next season. I think he's a longshot Rookie of the Year candidate simply because it's really hard to be a rookie catcher, and next year Salas will be the youngest regular catcher since Hall of Famer Ivan Rodriguez in 1991. Still, Salas is a special defender with promising offensive chops.

Several prominent Japanese veterans will make their way to MLB via the posting system this offseason. We don't know where they will sign yet, but the rules say these players will be Rookie of the Year-eligible regardless of their age or years of experience in Japan, so we're going to include them here.

We ranked Sato as the best position player free agent on the market this offseason. Japan's reigning Triple Crown winner has tremendous left-handed power. We're talking legitimate 30-homer upside. Sato does swing and miss a bunch, though, and he's an aggressive hitter who's unlikely to walk as much as Munetaka Murakami, which could hold him back at the plate. Add in questionable defense at the hot corner and it's unclear exactly how much impact Sato will have in the big leagues. Bottom line though, guys with 30-homer power will always be in the Rookie of the Year conversation.

Taira, our No. 19 free agent, is destined to be a fan favorite given his fire hydrant build (5-foot-8 and 220 lbs.) and bat-missing fastball. He gets close to seven feet of extension down the mound despite his height, creating a unique release window and an "upshoot" effect on his fastball. Taira started for the Seibu Lions in 2026 after spending 2024 and 2025 in the bullpen. I assume the team that signs him will give him a chance to start next year. If he winds up in relief, Taira has the stuff and gumption to get high-leverage outs in the late innings.

#2649. Bears Week 10 Flashbacks: Concannon’s Bombs, Dent’s Dominance, Vasher’s 108 yards

The Bears may be enjoying their bye week, but the Gridiron Time Machine doesn't need the week off.

Instead of our usual three games, we're digging a little deeper this week with five memorable Week 10 performances, spanning nearly 60 years of Bears history.

The 1967 Bears were sitting at 4-5 when the St. Louis Cardinals came to Wrigley Field for Week 10.

What followed was one of the more explosive passing performances of the era.

Jack Concannon completed only 11 passes, but those completions went for an incredible 336 yards and three touchdowns. Dick Gordon was responsible for most of the damage, catching four passes for 179 yards and two scores.

The touchdowns were not exactly short ones either.

Concannon connected with Gordon for a 93-yard touchdown early in the second quarter, then found Bob Jones for another 51-yard score. Before halftime arrived, Gordon struck again from 67 yards out.

Three touchdown passes. All three from more than 50 yards away.

Meanwhile, the Bears defense made sure St. Louis never had much of an opportunity to respond.

Chicago intercepted Cardinals quarterbacks seven times, including five picks from Jim Hart alone, while forcing nine turnovers overall. The Cardinals finished with only 230 total yards and never reached the end zone.

Chicago cruised to a 30-3 victory behind 461 yards of offense.

For a franchise that has not exactly been known for explosive passing attacks, Concannon throwing three touchdown passes of 51 yards or longer feels almost out of place in Bears history.

The Bears entered Week 10 of the 1979 season sitting at 4-5 and desperately trying to remain in the playoff picture.

Detroit turned out to be a pretty good opponent for getting things moving in the right direction.

Walter Payton once again carried the offense, rushing for 113 yards and two touchdowns on 22 carries while adding another 53 yards as a receiver. Mike Phipps threw for just 136 yards, but Chicago didn't need much through the air.

The fun really started in the third quarter.

With Chicago leading 14-7, Steve Schubert returned a punt 77 yards for a touchdown. Not long afterward, Terry Schmidt intercepted Lions quarterback Jeff Komlo and returned it 20 yards for another score.

Suddenly, a seven-point game had become a 28-7 Bears lead.

Payton added his second touchdown in the fourth quarter to finish off a 35-7 victory.

Chicago did not commit a turnover while forcing five from Detroit, and Payton finished with 166 yards from scrimmage. The win moved the Bears back to .500 at 5-5 and became part of a late-season push that eventually carried Chicago into the playoffs.

Give the ball to Walter Payton, let the defense create mistakes, and sneak in a special teams touchdown while you're at it.

One year before the 1985 Bears defense became immortal, Chicago was already showing the rest of the NFL what was coming.

The defending Super Bowl champion Los Angeles Raiders arrived at Soldier Field in Week 10 with a 7-2 record.

Walter Payton handled the offensive workload, rushing 27 times for 111 yards and scoring twice in the first half. His touchdown runs of 18 and eight yards gave Chicago a 14-0 advantage before the defense took care of everything else.

Dent recorded 4.5 sacks, which remains the Bears' single-game franchise record. Chicago sacked Raiders quarterbacks nine times overall, forced five turnovers and held Los Angeles to just 181 total yards.

The Raiders managed only two field goals in a 17-6 Bears victory. It was the first time the defending champions had been held without a touchdown in more than three years.

The win moved Chicago to 7-3 and gave the Bears another indication that Buddy Ryan's defense was developing into something special.

But before the Super Bowl Shuffle, the playoff shutouts and the legend of the 1985 defense, Richard Dent and company were already making Sundays miserable for opposing quarterbacks.

The defending Super Bowl champions just happened to get an early preview.

The Bears entered Week 10 of the 1990 season as one of the hottest teams in football.

Atlanta came to Soldier Field and nearly spoiled the afternoon.

After falling behind 3-0, Chicago scored 24 unanswered points behind touchdowns from Neal Anderson, Wendell Davis and Brad Muster. Jim Harbaugh connected with Davis for an eight-yard touchdown in the second quarter, and the Bears carried a 24-3 advantage into the second half.

Atlanta scored two unanswered touchdowns to cut the lead to 24-17, and what had looked like a comfortable afternoon suddenly became a one-score game.

Fortunately, Chris Miller threw one pass too many.

Vestee Jackson jumped the route and returned the interception 45 yards for a touchdown, pushing the lead back to 30-17 with just over a minute remaining. Atlanta scored once more, but Chicago held on for a 30-24 victory.

Miller threw for 239 yards and two touchdowns, but the Bears intercepted him four times. Wendell Davis led Chicago offensively with five catches for 105 yards and a score, while Harbaugh added 195 passing yards and another 47 on the ground.

The victory improved Chicago to 8-1 and extended its winning streak to five games.

Sometimes the defense dominates from start to finish.

Other times it waits until things get interesting before reminding everyone who is in charge.

If you remember anything about the Bears' 2005 Week 10 win over San Francisco, it probably isn't the offense.

Chicago quarterback Kyle Orton threw for only 67 yards. San Francisco quarterback Cody Pickett somehow managed just one completion for 28 yards.

With gusts approaching 50 miles per hour at Soldier Field, 49ers kicker Joe Nedney attempted a 52-yard field goal on the final play of the first half.

Vasher caught the ball deep in the end zone, briefly hesitated, then took off. He reversed field, found a convoy of blockers and raced all the way to the opposite end zone for a 108-yard touchdown.

At the time, it was the longest play in NFL history.

The return gave Chicago a 7-3 halftime lead in a game where points were extremely difficult to find. Adrian Peterson later rushed for a seven-yard touchdown and finished with 120 yards on 24 carries, while Robbie Gould added a fourth-quarter field goal.

The Bears held on for a 17-9 victory, their fifth straight win, improving to 6-3 while maintaining control of the NFC North.

One year later, Devin Hester would return another missed field goal exactly 108 yards against the Giants.

Apparently 108-yard missed field goal returns were just something Bears defensive backs did for a while.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

#2648. Sixers, Brown have a ‘humbling' night in loss to Celtics

Sixers, Brown have a 'humbling' night in loss to Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Whatever Jaylen Brown and the Sixers dreamed up for their first matchup against the Celtics soon flew out the window on Tuesday night.

Brown was whistled for two early fouls, the Sixers fell behind and their early-season flaws were on full display in a 123-101 loss at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"We've just got to get better," Brown said. "Tonight was humbling. We got outplayed, out-executed. So we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the next one."

Over 26 minutes, Brown had 13 points on 4-for-9 shooting and five rebounds against the team that traded him away this summer.

As for the endless dissection of his relationship with former co-star Jayson Tatum, Brown didn't have much to add Tuesday. There was no public reconciliation, no obvious on-court animosity and generally nothing to satisfy fans hoping for some kind of fireworks on that front.

"I'm just focused on doing what's best for my team," Brown said. "Everything else … to be honest, I wasn't paying attention. But credit to Jayson; he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics. They executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and they were the better team tonight."

Tatum scored 21 points, two of which came on a third-quarter slam over LeBron James. Paul George continued his fantastic start as a Celtic by dropping 36 points and draining six three-pointers.

The Celtics dominated from beyond the arc, shooting 22 for 49 (44.9 percent). The Sixers went just 11 for 37 (29.7 percent) on another night of underwhelming offense. The team sits 22nd in the NBA in offensive rating, 24th in three-point makes per game and 21st in three-point percentage.

"I think that we've got some guys that are obviously shooting much lower percentages than their last season or their career average — almost a handful of guys," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "And I don't think it's because they're shooting fallaway, totally contested ones. I think they're shots we want them to take. So I think they'll continue to take 'em and I'm pretty sure those will even out into their career averages."

Joel Embiid is at 37 percent from the floor and 4 for 33 from three-point range (12.1 percent).

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center got through an injury scare when he rolled his ankle late in the second quarter and hit a three early in the third. It was his first long-range make since the Sixers' home opener back on Oct. 22.

"It's a work in progress," Embiid said. "I think the biggest thing is just not thinking. I'm probably overthinking it. The rhythm of the game is different. I'm so used to having to create for myself, so it's a little bit different.

"But I think I'm slowly getting better. You could see as soon as I made a three, the next shot in the short corner … I didn't even think about it. I just shot it and let it fly, and I made it. … I think it's just about taking what's in front of you. Make or miss, keep working on your game. It's going to get there at some point."

Even with the Sixers second in the Eastern Conference standings at 9-3, Embiid believes the team's defense has "slacked off a little bit" in recent games.

"I don't really look at the record," he said. "I just look at the process of, 'Are we getting better every day?' We can always do a better job at all phases of the game."

"They're one of the top teams in the league and they've been together for a while," Brown said. "We've got a lot to work on over here, so we've got to get to work."

The Sixers will face the Raptors on Thursday night in Philadelphia.

They'll have to wait until Jan. 21 in Boston to see the Celtics again.

"I was looking forward to this," Brown said. "I was looking forward to playing well, but s— happens. Just get ready for the next one."

Tampa Bay attempts to complete a sweep of the 2026 ALDS when they square off against New York at 8 p.m. ET in Game 3 on Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The Rays, who defeated the Yankees in this round in 2020 en route to the second World Series appearance in franchise history, edged New York 1-0 in this year's series opener before pushing their AL East rivals to the brink of elimination with a 5-2 victory in Game 2.

The Rays went 7-6 against New York during the regular season but lost four of the six contests at Yankee Stadium, including three of four in their penultimate series of the campaign. Tampa Bay was outscored 15-6 in its final two games in the Bronx, but its pitching staff has kept the Yankees in check thus far in the ALDS.

New York was limited to one hit in Game 1 as Drew Rasmussen had a no-hitter for 7 2/3 innings before Austin Wells ripped a double down the right field line. However, Wells made an ill-advised decision to try and stretch it into a triple and was thrown out easily at third base. Rays closer Bryan Baker worked a perfect ninth to preserve the win.

The Yankees didn't fare much better offensively in Game 2 as they registered just four hits, two of which were solo homers by Ben Rice. They were even worse defensively, committing four errors -- including three in the first inning that helped give Tampa Bay a 1-0 lead.

Tampa Bay will look to punch its ticket to the ALCS behind Nick Martinez, who set a career high with 15 wins this year and matched another with a 3.10 ERA. #2646. 2026 MLB Rookie of the Year: Tigers' Kevin McGonigle, Reds' Sal Stewart win BBWAA awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Kevin McGonigle of the Tigers and Sal Stewart of the Reds were named the 2026 Rookies of the Year in their respective leagues on Monday night as part of the BBWAA's awards week. McGonigle earned 28 of 30 first-place votes, beating out the Guardians' Parker Messick and the Red Sox's Payton Tolle. Stewart, meanwhile, beat the Mets' Carson Benge and the Cardinals' JJ Wetherholt.

Because McGonigle and Stewart were both with the major-league team for long enough to earn a full year of service time, the Tigers and Reds will each receive a Prospect Promotion Incentive pick in the 2027 MLB Draft.

The annual awards, which also include Manager of the Year, Reliever of the Year, Cy Young and MVP, are voted on by 30 members of the Baseball Writers Association of America (that's two per MLB city in each league). Votes were submitted before the beginning of the playoffs, meaning that only regular-season contributions are taken into account.

Stewart won the battle of Old School stats vs. New School stats here. Though he only posted 2.0 WAR, he had 32 home runs and 111 RBI, putting him in rarefied air for a rookie. He's one of just 15 rookies ever with at least 30 homers and 100 RBI. The only names from that list to not win the award either faced another player from the list or played before Rookie of the Year was awarded. Everyone else has taken home the hardware, just as Stewart did Monday evening.

Overall, Stewart appeared in all 162 games, hitting .263/.330/.457 (117 OPS+) with 25 doubles, 32 homers, 112 RBI, 87 runs and 15 steals.

Stewart earned 20 of the 30 available first-place votes.

Carson Benge of the Mets finished second and JJ Wetherholt of the Cardinals finished in third place. Benge, the 2024 first-rounder, made the team out of spring training and hit .282/.346/.430 with 20 home runs, 22 steals and 4.3 WAR. Defensive metrics love Wetherholt and helped push him to 4.5 WAR in 139 games. He hit .242/.339/.365 with 17 homers, 14 steals and 89 runs.

Stewart joins the following Reds as Rookie of the Year winners:

The honor for McGonigle completes a stellar year for the former first-round draft pick. He broke camp with the Tigers and was productive from the get-go. He ended up hitting .278/.376/.430 (126 OPS+) with 28 doubles, five triples, 18 home runs, 72 RBI, 97 runs, 12 steals and 7.1 WAR, the latter good enough for the AL lead among position players. He played great defense, ran the bases well and was an All-Star. He nearly walked (95) as much as he struck out (100), too. Not much more could've been asked of the Pennsylvania native who played most of the season at age 21, and he's a well-deserving Rookie of the Year.

A few weeks after he debuted, he and the team agreed to an eight-year, $150 million extension.

McGonigle won in a blowout, getting 28 of the 30 available first-place votes, scoring 204 of a possible 210 points.

He joins the following players who have won the award with the Tigers:

Parker Messick of the Guardians finishes second after going 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings; he is also a top-three finalist for the Cy Young award. Red Sox starter Payton Tolle finishes third after going 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA (135 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 171 strikeouts in 148 ⅔ innings.
